abstract: Secure messaging now carries the most sensitive correspondence, credentials, and operational data of distributed enterprises, making these platforms high-value targets for data leakage, impersonation, and insider misuse. Although end-to-end encryption is widely deployed, three problems remain fragmented across the literature: authentication that still depends on optional, human-error-prone manual verification ceremonies and leaves an active man-in-the-middle gap; insider threats by users who already hold legitimate access; and an inherent tension between intelligent threat detection and the privacy that encryption is meant to preserve. This paper presents a structured literature review that synthesizes twelve recent studies across three domains: secure messaging and insider-threat detection, zero-knowledge authentication, and on-device artificial-intelligence detection. Characterizing each source by problem, method, findings, and limitations, the review extracts a key gap: no surveyed system unifies confidential transport, privacy-preserving authentication, and intelligent on-device detection within one mobile platform, and the privacy, feasibility, and trust tensions that arise only at their intersection remain unaddressed. Motivated by this gap, the review proposes SentriZK, a conceptual architecture for a privacy-preserving, mobile-first Android messenger that combines end-to-end encrypted transport, non-interactive zero-knowledge-proof authentication that replaces fragile fingerprint ceremonies, and lightweight on-device threat detection. The work is explicitly a literature review and a design-stage proposal; no experimental results for the proposed system are reported, and the review instead establishes the engineering agenda that subsequent implementation must resolve.
